title: The journey through the system
subtitle: MIAMs, the overriding objective, and private v public law process
objectives: State the MIAM requirement under s10 Children and Families Act 2014 and identify when it does and does not apply
Explain the Family Procedure Rules' overriding objective and how it shapes case management in family proceedings
Distinguish private law from public law family proceedings, and trace how a family client's dispute moves through the system from separation to final order

leadingAuthorities.role: Creates the requirement to attend a mediation information and assessment meeting before most family applications
States the overriding objective governing how family courts manage cases
Governs public law proceedings — the state's intervention to protect a child from significant harm

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Every other lesson in this module has taught you a substantive rule — what counts as a valid marriage, how financial remedies are calculated, when a child arrangements order is made. This lesson is different: it's the map of how a client actually gets from 'my relationship has broken down' to any of those outcomes. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You know the individual doctrines — this lesson checks whether you can place them correctly on the client's journey through the system.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans on scenario questions — is this client exempt from a MIAM, is this application private or public law — rather than bare definitions.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and take it slowly — the MIAM requirement and the overriding objective are procedural scaffolding for every substantive lesson in this module; get the terminology solid before working through the scenarios.

overview.hook: Everything else in this module has been about what the law says a family court can decide — how to divide assets, who gets parental responsibility, when adoption is proportionate. None of it tells you how a person with a broken relationship actually gets in front of a judge, or whether they even should. This lesson is the connective tissue: the process every one of those earlier lessons assumes is already running in the background.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 24 September 2026. The MIAM requirement and the Family Procedure Rules' overriding objective are settled procedural law. The move towards greater transparency in family courts is an active, expanding pilot programme rather than a uniform national rule as at the check date, and is flagged as such in Part 4.

parts.heading: Before you can apply: the MIAM requirement
parts.voice: structural — states the rule before its exceptions
body: Section 10 of the Children and Families Act 2014 requires a person to attend a family mediation information and assessment meeting — a MIAM — before making most family applications to court, covering both children applications (such as a child arrangements order) and financial remedy applications following divorce.

The policy behind this is straightforward: court is expensive, slow, and can be corrosive to an ongoing co-parenting relationship in a way that mediation often isn't. A MIAM isn't mediation itself — it's a short meeting with a trained mediator to explain what mediation involves and assess whether it's suitable for this particular dispute, so that court becomes a considered choice rather than a reflexive one.

But the requirement is not absolute. Family Procedure Rules Practice Direction 3A sets out a detailed list of exemptions — most importantly where there is evidence of domestic abuse meeting the prescribed criteria, where the case is urgent (for example, a risk of harm to a child or of assets being dissipated), where a previous MIAM has already been attended, or where there are ongoing child protection concerns. A solicitor's first job in a new matter is usually working out which of these, if any, applies.

components.text: Before making a relevant family application, a person must attend a family mediation information and assessment meeting, subject to the exceptions set out in Family Procedure Rules.
elements: Applies before most 'relevant family applications' (children and financial remedy applications)
Exemptions include evidence of domestic abuse meeting the prescribed criteria, urgency, prior MIAM attendance, and ongoing child protection concerns
The MIAM is an information and assessment meeting, not mediation itself

interaction.prompt: Is attendance at a MIAM compulsory before every private law family application?
options: No — Practice Direction 3A sets out recognised exemptions, including domestic abuse and urgency
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The MIAM requirement is the default, not an absolute rule — recognised exemptions exist precisely because mediation isn't appropriate, or safe, in every case.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The MIAM requirement is the default position, but Practice Direction 3A sets out recognised exemptions — most importantly domestic abuse evidence meeting the prescribed criteria, and urgency. It is not an absolute requirement in every case.

parts.heading: The overriding objective: how the rules tell courts to behave
parts.voice: structural — reference-style, building the framework the rest of the lesson assumes
body: Family Procedure Rules r1.1 sets the overriding objective: courts must deal with cases justly, having regard to any welfare issues involved. That last phrase is the distinctive feature of the family version of this idea — the civil procedure equivalent has no comparable requirement, because civil litigation doesn't typically involve a vulnerable third party (the child) whose interests the court must keep in view even when they aren't a formal party to the case.

'Justly' is then broken down into familiar case-management goals: dealing with cases in ways that are proportionate to the nature, importance and complexity of the issues; ensuring the parties are on an equal footing; saving expense; and dealing with cases expeditiously and fairly, while allotting the court an appropriate share of its resources given the needs of other cases.

This isn't abstract. It's the rule that lets a judge actively manage a case — narrowing the issues, restricting expert evidence, setting a timetable — rather than simply refereeing whatever the parties choose to argue about, and it's the rule a court leans on whenever a case threatens to become disproportionately expensive or slow relative to what's actually at stake for the family and, especially, for any children involved.

components.label: FPR r1.1: the overriding objective
points: Dealing with cases justly, having regard to any welfare issues involved — the distinctively family-law element
Proportionate to the nature, importance and complexity of the issues
Ensuring the parties are on an equal footing
Dealing with the case expeditiously and fairly
Allotting to the case an appropriate share of the court's resources, while taking account of the need to allot resources to other cases

interaction.prompt: Which phrase in FPR r1.1's overriding objective explicitly distinguishes it from the equivalent civil procedure objective?
options: Having regard to any welfare issues involved
Dealing with the case expeditiously and fairly
Ensuring the parties are on an equal footing
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Proportionality, equal footing, expedition and resource-allotment all have direct civil procedure counterparts — the welfare limb is the addition unique to family proceedings, reflecting the child's interests that so often sit behind them.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Proportionality, equal footing and expedition are shared with civil procedure's overriding objective. The genuinely distinctive family-law addition is the requirement to have regard to any welfare issues involved.

parts.heading: Private law and public law: two different journeys through the same system
body: Almost everything covered earlier in this module — divorce, financial remedies, child arrangements, non-molestation orders — is private law: proceedings between family members, initiated by one of them, in which the state is not itself a party seeking an outcome (even though the court, and often Cafcass, plays an active role).

Public law is different in kind, not just in name. It means the state, through a local authority, applies to intervene in family life to protect a child — principally through care or supervision proceedings under Part IV of the Children Act 1989. A local authority can only bring such proceedings where it can establish the threshold criteria under s31: that the child is suffering, or is likely to suffer, significant harm, and that the harm (or likelihood of it) is attributable to the care given to the child not being what it would be reasonable to expect a parent to give.

The adoption process from the previous lesson sits at the intersection of the two: it can arise from a purely private arrangement (a step-parent adoption, for instance) or follow directly from public law care proceedings where a local authority's care plan is adoption. Recognising which track a case sits on — and therefore which parties, which threshold test, and which procedural rules apply — is the first thing a family lawyer needs to establish about any new matter.

components.title: Private law or public law? A decision path
components.description: A flowchart distinguishing the two proceedings tracks by who is bringing the application and why.

nodes.label: Is a local authority applying to protect a child from harm?
Yes → public law: Children Act 1989 Part IV, s 31 threshold criteria apply
No → private law: a family member applies (divorce, financial remedy, child arrangements, protective orders)

components.textAlternative: Ask first whether a local authority is applying to protect a child from harm. If so, the case is public law, governed by Part IV Children Act 1989 and the s31 threshold criteria. If not — if the application is brought by a family member over a family dispute such as divorce, a financial remedy, child arrangements, or a protective order — the case is private law.

interaction.prompt: Which of these is a public law family proceeding?
interaction.scenarioA: A mother applies to the family court for a child arrangements order setting out how much time her son spends with his father after their separation.
interaction.scenarioB: A local authority applies for a care order, having assessed that a child is suffering significant harm attributable to the care given by his parents.
interaction.explanation: Scenario B is public law: the state, through the local authority, is the applicant, and the case turns on the s31 threshold criteria. Scenario A is private law — a dispute between family members about a child arrangements order, with no local authority seeking to intervene.

parts.heading: Transparency: family courts opening up, carefully
parts.voice: reflective — engages directly with an unsettled, moving policy question
body: Family proceedings involving children have traditionally been held largely in private, and reporting has been tightly restricted — a deliberate trade-off in favour of protecting children's privacy over the open-justice principle that governs most other courts. Critics have long argued this comes at a cost: it makes it harder to scrutinise how the family justice system actually treats the families that pass through it.

Since 2023, transparency reporting pilots have allowed accredited journalists and legal bloggers to attend and report on certain family proceedings, subject to strict anonymity provisions protecting the identities of children and, usually, the adults involved. Where the pilot applies, the shift is real: cases that would once have been entirely invisible to the public can now be reported, with the underlying facts made public while identifying details are stripped out.

But this remains a piloted and expanding programme, not a uniform national rule covering every family court and every type of case. Students should resist the assumption that family justice has simply 'become open' — the correct, current position is that transparency is increasing through a specific, evolving reform process, and its scope should be checked against the latest guidance for any particular court or case type rather than assumed.

components.definition: A programme, beginning in 2023 and expanding since, under which accredited media and legal bloggers may attend and report on specified family proceedings subject to strict safeguards protecting the anonymity of children and, typically, the adults involved — a piloted reform, not (as at the check date) a universal rule applying to every family court.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that every family court in England and Wales now permits full, unrestricted media reporting of children proceedings?
sliderLabels: Not confident — this is still a piloted, expanding programme with anonymity safeguards
Confident — this is now a uniform national rule
interaction.correctPosition: Not confident — this is still a piloted, expanding programme with anonymity safeguards
interaction.explanation: Correct to be cautious. Transparency reporting is expanding through specific pilots with strict anonymity safeguards, not through a single uniform rule applied everywhere — treat the scope of reporting access as something to check for the specific court and case type, not assume.

parts.heading: The client's journey: pulling it together
parts.voice: reflective — synthesising, closes the module's process lesson
body: Put the pieces together and a typical private law journey looks like this: a relationship breaks down; unless an exemption applies, the person seeking to resolve a dispute over finances or children attends a MIAM; if mediation isn't suitable or doesn't resolve things, an application is made to court — a no-fault divorce application running on its own statutory timetable (Lesson 3), a financial remedy application applying the s25 checklist and the sharing/needs/compensation strands (Lessons 4–6), or a child arrangements application applying the welfare checklist (Lesson 9). Throughout, the court manages the case under the overriding objective, weighing welfare alongside proportionality and expense.

Where domestic abuse is present, the journey changes: a MIAM exemption is likely to apply, and the client may need urgent protective orders (Lesson 11) running alongside, or instead of, the substantive application. And if at any point a local authority becomes concerned enough about a child's safety to intervene, the case can shift entirely onto the public law track — a different applicant, a different threshold test, and potentially the route towards adoption or special guardianship covered in Lesson 13.

This lesson doesn't add a new area of substantive law to the module — it's the spine that the other fourteen lessons hang off. A student who can place divorce, financial remedies, children's orders, domestic abuse protection and adoption correctly onto this procedural map has understood not just what family law says, but how a family actually experiences it.

components.label: A private law client's route through the system
points: Separation → MIAM (unless exempt, e.g. domestic abuse or urgency)
Mediation unsuccessful or unsuitable → application to court (divorce, financial remedy, and/or child arrangements, as relevant)
Case management under the FPR overriding objective, with regard to welfare issues throughout
Domestic abuse present → protective orders may run alongside or instead of the substantive application, often bypassing the MIAM requirement
Local authority child protection concerns arise → case may shift onto the public law track, with adoption or special guardianship as possible outcomes

interaction.prompt: Put these stages of a typical private law family dispute in the order they usually occur.
items: The relationship breaks down and the parties separate
The applicant attends a MIAM (unless an exemption applies)
An application is made to the family court
The court manages the case under the overriding objective and makes a final order
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the private law spine: separation, the MIAM gateway, the application itself, and case management under the overriding objective through to a final order — the sequence every other lesson in this module ultimately plugs into.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — the MIAM requirement sits between separation and the application to court, not after it, because its purpose is to divert suitable cases away from court before they get there.

testPool.prompt: State the statutory basis for the MIAM requirement.
testPool.modelAnswer: Section 10 of the Children and Families Act 2014, which requires attendance at a family mediation information and assessment meeting before most family applications, subject to the exemptions in Family Procedure Rules Practice Direction 3A.

testPool.prompt: Name the Family Procedure Rules provision that states the overriding objective governing family proceedings.
testPool.modelAnswer: Rule 1.1 of the Family Procedure Rules 2010, which requires the court to deal with cases justly, having regard to any welfare issues involved.

testPool.prompt: Can a party with clear evidence of domestic abuse meeting the prescribed criteria skip the MIAM requirement before applying to court?
options: Yes — this is a recognised exemption under Practice Direction 3A
No — MIAM attendance is required in every case regardless of domestic abuse

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is a recognised MIAM exemption under Family Procedure Rules Practice Direction 3A?
options: Evidence of domestic abuse meeting the prescribed criteria
The applicant simply prefers not to attend
The respondent lives in a different part of the country
testPool.trapExplanation: A bare preference to skip the meeting, or the respondent living elsewhere, are not recognised exemptions — Practice Direction 3A lists specific, evidence-based grounds such as domestic abuse, urgency, prior MIAM attendance and ongoing child protection concerns.

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, highlight the sentence that states the public law threshold test.
testPool.passage: Public law proceedings are brought by a local authority seeking to protect a child, not by one family member against another. Before a care or supervision order can be made, the court must be satisfied that the child is suffering, or is likely to suffer, significant harm, and that the harm or likelihood of harm is attributable to the care given to the child not being what it would be reasonable to expect a parent to give. Only once that threshold is crossed does the court go on to consider what order, if any, best serves the child's welfare.
testPool.ratioSentence: Before a care or supervision order can be made, the court must be satisfied that the child is suffering, or is likely to suffer, significant harm, and that the harm or likelihood of harm is attributable to the care given to the child not being what it would be reasonable to expect a parent to give.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that identifies this as a public law, rather than private law, proceeding.
testPool.scenarioText: Following an anonymous referral, a local authority carries out an assessment of a family and concludes that a child is suffering significant harm attributable to parental neglect. It applies to the family court for a care order, naming the parents as respondents.
tappableSpans: a local authority carries out an assessment
applies to the family court for a care order
testPool.correctSpan: applies to the family court for a care order
testPool.explanation: What makes a case public law is who applies and for what: a local authority applying for a care order, invoking the state's power to intervene under Part IV Children Act 1989. The assessment and referral are background steps; the application itself is the defining fact.

testPool.prompt: Which client is more clearly exempt from the MIAM requirement before applying to court?
testPool.scenarioA: A client wants to apply for a child arrangements order and has a recent police disclosure confirming a domestic abuse incident against her by the respondent, meeting the prescribed evidential criteria.
testPool.scenarioB: A client wants to apply for a child arrangements order and simply feels mediation would be a waste of time given how badly the relationship ended.
testPool.explanation: Documented domestic abuse evidence meeting the prescribed criteria is a recognised exemption under Practice Direction 3A. A personal view that mediation would be pointless, without more, is not an exemption — that client is still expected to attend a MIAM.

testPool.prompt: A client alleges her former partner has been controlling and coercive and provides a recent, prescribed form of evidence to that effect. She wants to apply immediately for a non-molestation order. Must she attend a MIAM first?
options: No — evidence of domestic abuse meeting the prescribed criteria is a recognised exemption, and urgency also supports proceeding straight to court
Yes — MIAM attendance is required before any application, regardless of urgency or abuse
No — non-molestation orders are never subject to the MIAM requirement, whatever the facts
testPool.explanation: Both the domestic abuse exemption and, often, urgency apply here — the correct answer identifies the domestic abuse evidence as the operative exemption, rather than suggesting non-molestation applications are categorically outside the MIAM regime altogether.

testPool.prompt: A local authority believes a child is at risk of significant harm because of a parent's untreated substance dependency and wants to intervene formally. Which procedural framework governs its application?
options: Children Act 1989, Part IV, applying the s31 threshold criteria
The private law child arrangements framework under s8 Children Act 1989
The MIAM regime under s10 Children and Families Act 2014
testPool.explanation: A local authority seeking to intervene to protect a child from significant harm is on the public law track, governed by Part IV Children Act 1989 and the s31 threshold — not the private law child arrangements framework, and not the MIAM regime, which applies to private law applications between family members.

testPool.prompt: A client separated from her partner three months ago. There is no evidence of domestic abuse or urgency. She wants to apply immediately for both a financial remedy and a child arrangements order without attending a MIAM, believing it will simply delay matters. Analyse whether she can lawfully do so.
factsToOrder: The relevant applications are a financial remedy application and a child arrangements order
No domestic abuse evidence or urgency is present
The client wishes to bypass the MIAM requirement purely to save time

scaffolds.support: Full model answer shown, mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule given; student applies it to the facts and writes the conclusion
No scaffold; student writes the full analysis unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the client must attend a MIAM under s10 Children and Families Act 2014 before making her intended applications.
modelAnswer.rule: s10 requires attendance at a MIAM before most relevant family applications, including financial remedy and children applications, subject to the exemptions set out in Family Procedure Rules Practice Direction 3A (such as domestic abuse evidence, urgency, prior MIAM attendance, or child protection concerns).
modelAnswer.application: On these facts, no domestic abuse evidence or urgency is present, and none of the other recognised exemptions apply. A wish to save time is not itself a recognised ground for exemption.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The client must attend a MIAM before making either application; she cannot lawfully bypass the requirement simply because she believes it will delay matters.

testPool.prompt: Order the typical stages of a financial remedy application after divorce.
items: Form A application is filed with the court
Final hearing, if the matter has not settled

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that public law proceedings under Part IV Children Act 1989 must always be brought by a local authority, rather than a private individual?
sliderLabels: Confident — a local authority must be the applicant
testPool.correctPosition: Confident — a local authority must be the applicant
testPool.explanation: Correct. Care and supervision proceedings under Part IV are, by definition, brought by a local authority (or, in narrow circumstances, an authorised person) — that is precisely what distinguishes public law from a private family member's own application.

testPool.prompt: Which statement best reflects the current, correct position on transparency in family courts as at the check date?
options: Reporting access is expanding through specific, evolving pilots with anonymity safeguards, not through a single uniform national rule
All family proceedings are now open to unrestricted media reporting
Family courts remain entirely closed to all media reporting in every case
testPool.trapExplanation: Both extremes are wrong. Family courts were never entirely closed to all reporting (restricted reporting is not the same as no reporting), and the transparency pilots have not produced a uniform, unrestricted national rule — the accurate position is an expanding, piloted, safeguarded reform still in progress.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is conflating the private law and public law tracks — treating 'the state is involved somewhere' (a Cafcass report, a court hearing) as equivalent to a local authority actually being the applicant. The second most common: assuming a personal preference to avoid mediation counts as a recognised MIAM exemption, when only the specific, evidence-based grounds in Practice Direction 3A do.
